questions.prompt: An investor places a stop-limit sell order with a stop price of $48 and a limit price of $47.50 on a stock currently trading at $50. The stock falls and trades at $48. What happens to the order?
options: It becomes a limit order to sell at $47.50 or better, which may or may not fill depending on available prices
It becomes a market order and fills immediately at whatever price is available
It is cancelled automatically because the stop price was reached
Nothing happens until the limit price is also separately triggered by the stock falling to $47.50
questions.explain: A stop-limit order uses the same trigger as a plain stop order, but once the stop price is touched it becomes a limit order rather than a market order — it gives price protection at the cost of a guarantee that it fills at all. Reaching $48 activates the order as a limit sell at $47.50, which only fills if the market actually trades there or better.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the exchange rule that fills better-priced orders first, and among orders at the same price fills whichever arrived first, is called ________ priority.
questions.explain: Price-time priority means a better price is always filled first, and among orders resting at the exact same price, the order that arrived first gets filled first — which discourages constantly canceling and replacing an order just to cut in line.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about why a market maker's bid-ask spread exists, per the market microstructure lesson.
options: It compensates for order-processing costs, the operational cost of handling a trade
It compensates for inventory risk from holding a position between trades
It compensates for adverse selection, the risk of trading against better-informed counterparties
It is set purely by exchange regulation and has nothing to do with the market maker's own risk
It always narrows during periods of high volatility and uncertainty
questions.explain: The spread compensates for three distinct risks: order-processing cost, inventory risk, and adverse selection. It is not a regulatory mandate but a reflection of the market maker's own risk-bearing, and spreads widen (not narrow) in volatile or uncertain conditions, since inventory risk and adverse selection both rise.

questions.prompt: Match each liquidity-related concept to what it actually measures.
right: The price movement caused by a trader's own large order
How much size rests near the best bid and ask
How narrow the bid-ask spread is
How quickly the order book refills after a large trade
questions.explain: Tightness is how narrow the spread is; depth is how much size rests near the top of the book; resiliency is how quickly the book and price recover after a large trade; market impact is the price movement a trader's own large order causes by walking through multiple price levels.

questions.prompt: What does a bond's yield to maturity (YTM) represent?
options: The single discount rate that makes the present value of all the bond's remaining coupons and face value equal to its current market price
The bond's stated annual coupon rate, expressed as a percent of face value
The total dollar amount of coupons the bond will pay over its remaining life
The current yield, calculated as the annual coupon divided by the bond's current price
The bond's credit rating expressed as a numerical score
The percentage change in a bond's price for a 1 percentage-point change in interest rates
questions.explain: Yield to maturity is the single discount rate that equates the present value of every remaining coupon payment and the final face-value repayment to the bond's current market price — the bond market's way of expressing the return you'd earn holding the bond to maturity and reinvesting every coupon at that same rate.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D, current yield, is a real and related bond metric — annual coupon divided by current price — but it only looks at one year's income against today's price. It ignores the time value and timing of every other future cash flow and the eventual repayment of face value, which is exactly what YTM accounts for by discounting every remaining payment back to today.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ________ duration converts Macaulay duration into a direct estimate of the percentage price change for a 1 percentage-point change in yield.
questions.explain: Modified duration adjusts Macaulay duration (Macaulay Duration divided by (1 + y)) into a direct sensitivity measure — the approximate percentage price change a bond experiences for a 1 percentage-point move in yield.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the differences between forwards and futures.
options: Futures are marked to market daily, with gains and losses settled through a margin account
Forwards are standardized contracts traded on a regulated exchange
Futures are cleared through a central counterparty, which largely eliminates counterparty risk
A forward contract settles only once, at expiration
Forwards carry less counterparty risk than futures because they are privately negotiated
questions.explain: Futures are marked to market daily through margin accounts and cleared through a CCP, which largely eliminates counterparty risk. Forwards are the opposite of standardized exchange contracts — they are bespoke, OTC, bilateral agreements that settle only once at expiration, and that bespoke, uncleared structure means forwards carry MORE counterparty risk than futures, not less.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of pricing the 3-year, 6% coupon bond at an 8% yield to maturity (Lesson 8's worked example) in the correct order.
items: Identify each future cash flow: $60 in years 1 and 2, and $1,060 in year 3
Discount each cash flow back to today at the 8% yield to maturity
Sum the three discounted cash flows to get the bond's price of $948.00
Compare the price to face value to confirm the bond trades at a discount because the coupon rate is below the yield
questions.explain: Bond pricing always proceeds this way: lay out every future cash flow, discount each one back to today at the yield, sum the discounted amounts into the price, and then the resulting price can be compared to face value — here $948.00 sits below the $1,000 face value because the 6% coupon is below the 8% yield to maturity, so the bond must trade at a discount.

questions.code:
S, K, premium = 54, 50, 3
payoff = max(S - K, 0)
profit = payoff - premium
questions.prompt: A trader buys one call option with strike K = $50 for a premium of $3. At expiration the stock is trading at S = $54. What is the trader's profit per share?
options: $1, because the payoff of $4 minus the $3 premium paid leaves a $1 profit
$4, the option's payoff at expiration, since profit and payoff are the same thing
$3, equal to the premium paid
−$3, because the option expired worthless and the full premium was lost
questions.explain: The call's payoff at expiration is max(S − K, 0) = max(54 − 50, 0) = $4. Profit for the buyer is payoff minus the premium paid: 4 − 3 = $1. The option is in the money with real payoff, but profit still has to subtract what was originally paid for the right.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: put-call parity states C − P = S − K·e^(−rT), where K·e^(−rT) represents the ________ of the strike price paid at expiration.
acceptedAnswers: present value of the strike price
questions.explain: K·e^(−rT) discounts the strike price back from expiration to today at the continuously compounded risk-free rate — it is the present value of the cash that will be paid to exercise the option at expiration, which is exactly the quantity the replicating-portfolio argument needs on both sides of the parity equation.

questions.prompt: Select every assumption the Black-Scholes model makes, per the lesson on the model.
options: The stock price follows geometric Brownian motion, with lognormally distributed returns
Volatility and the risk-free rate are constant over the life of the option
Markets are frictionless, with no transaction costs and unrestricted short-selling
The option can be exercised at any time up to and including expiration
Trading is continuous, allowing costless continuous rebalancing of a hedging portfolio
questions.explain: Black-Scholes assumes lognormal, geometric-Brownian-motion returns, constant volatility and risk-free rate, frictionless markets, and continuous trading with costless rebalancing. It explicitly assumes the OPPOSITE of early exercise: the option is European-style, exercisable only at expiration — early exercise is the American-option case the binomial tree handles instead.

questions.prompt: What is a European call option's payoff at expiration, where S is the underlying's price and K is the strike price?
options: max(S − K, 0)
max(K − S, 0)
S − K, even when that value is negative
max(S − K, 0) minus the premium originally paid
max(S, K)
min(S − K, 0)
questions.explain: A call is only worth exercising if the market price S is above the strike K — otherwise you'd rather buy at the lower market price, so the right is worthless. That makes the payoff max(S − K, 0): zero when the option is out of the money, and S − K whenever it finishes above the strike.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B, max(K − S, 0), is the put payoff formula, not the call — it simply swaps which side of S and K is subtracted. A put is the right to sell, which pays off when the underlying falls below the strike, the mirror image of a call. Mixing up max(S−K,0) and max(K−S,0) is the single most common payoff-formula error.

questions.prompt: Match each Greek to what it measures.
right: Sensitivity to the passage of time
The rate of change of delta itself as the underlying moves
Sensitivity to a $1 move in the underlying
questions.explain: Delta (∂V/∂S) measures sensitivity to a $1 move in the underlying. Gamma (∂Delta/∂S) measures how fast delta itself changes. Vega (∂V/∂σ) measures sensitivity to volatility. Theta (∂V/∂t) measures sensitivity to the passage of time — typically negative for a long option position.

questions.prompt: Equity index options typically show higher implied volatility for low strikes than for high strikes. What is the usual explanation for this skew?
options: Investors bid up the price of out-of-the-money puts for downside/crash protection, which raises their implied volatility relative to higher strikes
Low-strike options are always more liquid, which mechanically raises their quoted implied volatility
The Black-Scholes formula itself assigns a higher theoretical volatility to options with lower strikes
Low-strike options have less time value remaining, which inflates their implied volatility
questions.explain: The usual explanation for the equity index skew is demand for downside protection: investors buy puts to hedge against crashes, bidding up the price — and therefore the implied volatility — of low-strike options relative to what a constant-volatility Black-Scholes world would predict. Black-Scholes itself assumes one flat volatility for every strike; the skew is direct market evidence that assumption doesn't hold.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of pricing an option via binomial backward induction in the correct order.
items: Build the tree of possible up and down stock price moves out to expiration
Compute the option's payoff at every final node at expiration
Discount the risk-neutral expected value of each node's two successors back one step
Repeat the discounting step backward, layer by layer, until reaching today's single node
questions.explain: Binomial pricing builds the tree of up/down moves first, computes the known payoff at every final node, then works backward one layer at a time, discounting the risk-neutral expected value of each node's two successors, repeating until a single value at today's node emerges as the option's fair price.

questions.prompt: Two assets have standard deviations of 20% and 30% and a correlation of 0.3. If combined in equal weights, how does the portfolio's standard deviation compare to the simple weighted average of the two individual standard deviations (25%)?
options: It is lower than 25%, because the correlation is below 1, making the cross term in the portfolio variance formula smaller than it would be at perfect correlation
It equals exactly 25%, since weighted averages always apply directly to standard deviation
It is higher than 25%, because combining two risky assets always increases total risk
It cannot be determined without also knowing each asset's expected return
questions.explain: Portfolio variance is w1²σ1² + w2²σ2² + 2w1w2ρσ1σ2, not a simple weighted average of standard deviations. Because ρ = 0.3 is below 1, the cross term is smaller than it would be under perfect correlation, and the resulting portfolio standard deviation (about 20.4% in this exact example from Lesson 18) comes out below the naive 25% weighted average — that gap is the diversification benefit.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in CAPM, beta is calculated as the covariance between an asset's return and the market's return, divided by the ________ of the market's return.
questions.explain: Beta_i = Cov(Ri, Rm) / Var(Rm) — the covariance between the asset and the market, scaled by the market's own variance. This isolates how sensitive an asset's returns are to market-wide moves, independent of the asset's own total volatility.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM).
options: Only systematic risk earns a return premium under CAPM, because unsystematic risk can be diversified away
The Security Market Line plots expected return against beta, and every correctly priced asset sits on it under CAPM
The Capital Market Line plots expected return against total risk (sigma) and only describes efficient portfolios
A stock's own standard deviation is the risk measure CAPM uses to determine its expected return
Beta isolates the systematic component of an asset's risk, separate from its unsystematic risk
questions.explain: CAPM compensates only systematic risk, since unsystematic risk is diversifiable. The Security Market Line graphs expected return against beta and every correctly priced asset sits on it; the Capital Market Line graphs expected return against total risk and only describes efficient portfolios. CAPM deliberately uses beta rather than an asset's own standard deviation, because sigma mixes systematic and unsystematic risk together, while beta isolates just the systematic piece.

questions.prompt: Match each performance-attribution measure to how it is calculated.
right: Excess return divided by total risk (standard deviation)
Active return divided by tracking error against a specific benchmark
Actual return minus the return CAPM would have predicted given the portfolio's beta
questions.explain: Sharpe ratio divides excess return by total risk; Treynor ratio divides excess return by beta; Jensen's alpha subtracts the CAPM-predicted return from the actual return; and the information ratio divides active return (versus a specific benchmark) by tracking error.

questions.prompt: A portfolio's 1-day 99% Value at Risk (VaR) is reported as $2 million. What does this statement actually mean?
options: On no more than 1% of trading days, the portfolio is expected to lose more than $2 million — it does not mean losses can never exceed $2 million
The portfolio can never lose more than $2 million in a single day
The portfolio is expected to lose exactly $2 million on 99% of trading days
The average loss on the worst 1% of trading days is $2 million
questions.explain: VaR at a given confidence level and horizon is the loss level not expected to be exceeded with that probability. A 1-day 99% VaR of $2 million means losses beyond $2 million are supposed to be rare — about a 1-in-100-day event — not that they are impossible. Option D describes Expected Shortfall, a related but different measure that reports the average loss beyond the VaR threshold.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: expected credit loss is estimated as Probability of Default multiplied by Loss Given Default multiplied by ________.
questions.explain: Expected credit loss is roughly PD × LGD × EAD — the likelihood of default, the fraction of exposure actually lost if default happens, and the amount owed at the moment of default, multiplied together.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES).
options: VaR says nothing about how severe a loss is once it exceeds the VaR threshold
VaR is guaranteed to be sub-additive, meaning combining two positions can never increase total risk beyond the sum of their individual VaRs
Expected Shortfall reports the average loss in the scenarios beyond the VaR threshold
Regulators moved minimum trading-book capital requirements toward a 97.5% Expected Shortfall measure under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
Parametric (variance-covariance) VaR assumes portfolio returns are normally distributed
questions.explain: VaR is tail-blind (silent on severity beyond the threshold) and is NOT guaranteed sub-additive — combining positions can sometimes raise VaR above the sum of its parts, which is exactly one of its two well-known limitations. Expected Shortfall fixes this by averaging losses beyond the threshold and is a coherent (sub-additive) measure, which is why FRTB moved capital rules to a 97.5% ES standard. Parametric VaR specifically relies on a normality assumption.

questions.prompt: Put these layers of the "three lines of defense" risk governance model in order, from closest to the risk-taking itself to most independent oversight.
items: The business line that takes the risk and owns it day to day
An independent risk and compliance function that sets limits and monitors the business line
Internal audit, which periodically verifies the first two lines are functioning as designed
questions.explain: The three lines of defense run from the business line (which takes and owns the risk day to day), to an independent risk and compliance function (which sits apart, sets limits, and monitors the business line), to internal audit (which periodically verifies both earlier lines are actually functioning as designed, independent of both).

questions.prompt: How does a proprietary trading firm differ from a hedge fund?
options: A proprietary trading firm trades its own capital with no outside investors, while a hedge fund exists specifically to manage outside investors' money
A proprietary trading firm only trades fixed income, while hedge funds only trade equities
A proprietary trading firm charges a 2 and 20 fee structure while hedge funds do not
A proprietary trading firm is always larger, by assets under management, than a hedge fund
questions.explain: Proprietary trading firms trade the firm's own capital — there's no fund to raise and no investor reporting. A hedge fund's whole business model is managing outside investors' money, typically charging management and performance fees on it. Neither firm type is defined by trading a single asset class, and the 2-and-20 fee model belongs to hedge funds, not prop shops.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a quant ________ designs and backtests trading signals and models, leaning heaviest on statistics, probability, and machine learning, while a quant developer leans heaviest on software engineering.
questions.explain: A quant researcher forms a hypothesis about a market pattern, builds a model to capture it, and rigorously backtests whether it would have worked historically — leaning heaviest on statistics, probability, and machine learning, distinct from the quant developer's software-engineering focus and the quant trader's live-execution focus.

questions.prompt: Match each type of firm to what it actually does.
right: Primarily services client order flow while taking on some proprietary risk within regulatory limits
Trades its own capital, with no outside investors to raise money from or report to
Pools capital from qualified investors and pursues strategies such as long/short equity or global macro
Runs long-only mandates benchmarked against an index such as the S&P 500
questions.explain: A hedge fund pools outside investors' capital and pursues varied strategies. A proprietary trading firm trades only its own capital. An investment bank trading desk mainly services client order flow while taking on limited proprietary risk. An asset manager or pension fund runs long-only, benchmark-relative mandates.

questions.prompt: The capstone's ZQX options portfolio has a net delta of approximately +979 shares-equivalent. What hedge trade flattens the portfolio's delta to zero?
options: Sell short approximately 979 shares of ZQX
Buy approximately 979 shares of ZQX
Sell short approximately 1,958 shares of ZQX
No trade is needed, since delta always nets to zero across a mix of long and short options
questions.explain: The hedge trade in shares is simply −portfolio delta. With a portfolio delta of about +979, selling short approximately 979 shares of ZQX brings the combined position's net delta close to zero, since each share of stock carries a delta of exactly 1.

questions.prompt: After the capstone's delta-hedge trade, select every statement that is true about the portfolio's remaining risk.
options: The portfolio still has nonzero gamma, so its delta will drift away from zero as ZQX's price moves
The portfolio still has nonzero vega, so it still has exposure to changes in implied volatility
The hedge trade in shares has zero vega, since a share of stock has no sensitivity to volatility
The delta-hedge, once put on, never needs to be rebalanced again
A real trading desk would need to rebalance this hedge periodically because gamma causes the hedge to drift out of date
questions.explain: Flattening delta does nothing about gamma (≈+17.7) or vega (≈+$163 per vol point), both of which remain exposed. Because gamma is nonzero, the portfolio's delta drifts away from zero as ZQX moves, so the hedge needs periodic rebalancing rather than being set once — the opposite of the false claim that it never needs rebalancing. A share of stock has zero vega, so the hedge trade itself does nothing to offset the remaining vega exposure.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: when aggregating each option's Greek to the portfolio level, the capstone multiplies each option's per-share Greek by its position size and by the ________ convention of 100 shares per contract.
questions.explain: Each option's per-share Greek is scaled by position size (positive for long, negative for short) and by the contract multiplier — the standard convention that one option contract covers 100 shares of the underlying — before being summed into the portfolio-level Greek.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the capstone project in the order they are carried out across the Capstone Kickoff, Build It, and Wrap-Up lessons.
items: Define the fictional ZQX Inc. portfolio of three options with their strikes, maturities, and implied vols
Price each option and compute its delta, gamma, and vega using the Black-Scholes formulas
Aggregate each option's Greek across the portfolio, scaled by position size and contract multiplier
Size a hedge trade in ZQX shares that flattens the portfolio's net delta to zero
Review what gamma and vega exposure remains, and explain why the hedge needs periodic rebalancing
questions.explain: The capstone runs in exactly this sequence: set up the portfolio and its market inputs, price each option and its Greeks, aggregate those Greeks to the portfolio level, size the delta-flattening hedge trade, and finally review what risk remains (gamma and vega) and why a real desk would need to rebalance the hedge over time.
